hafez: Khajeh Shams-od-Din Mohammad Hafez Shirazi was born in Shiraz and identified as a Sufi Muslim. Few details of his life are known, and accounts of his early years rely on traditional anecdotes; the early tazkiras, or biographical sketches, that mention him are generally considered unreliable. He is said to have memorized the Quran at an early age, and the title Hafez, which he later used as his pen name, was given to him for this.

He was supported by the patronage of several successive local regimes, among them Shah Abu Ishaq, who came to power while Hafez was in his teens, and the strict Mubariz ud-Din Muhammad. His work flourished most under the 27-year rule of Jalal ud-Din Shah Shuja. Hafez also exchanged letters and poetry with Ghiyasuddin Azam Shah, the Sultan of Bengal, who invited him to Sonargaon; he could not go.

Hafez wrote chiefly lyric poetry in the form of the ghazal. His Divan, probably compiled after his death, deals with the beloved, faith, wine and taverns, and the exposure of hypocrisy. Whether the poems are to be read literally, mystically or both has been disputed. William Jones saw a conventional lyricist like Petrarch, Henry Wilberforce Clarke a poet of ecstatic mysticism like Rumi, and Ralph Waldo Emerson rejected the Sufi reading of wine. The argument arises because early Persian poetic vocabulary was taken over by mystics, so that no 14th-century lyric could avoid a mystical flavour; Hafez embraced the fusion.

According to an account by Jami, Hafez died in 1390. Twenty years later a tomb was raised for him in the Musalla Gardens in Shiraz; the present mausoleum was designed by André Godard in the late 1930s. There is no definitive version of the Divan: editions run from 573 to 994 poems. Hafez was acclaimed across the Islamic world in his lifetime, and William Jones first translated him into English in 1771. In Iran families open the Divan at random on Nowruz and Yalda Night and read the poem as a sign of what will come.
hagia-sophia: Justinian's building was the third church on the site. The first, known as the Magna Ecclesia, or Great Church, because of its size, was consecrated on 15 February 360 under the emperor Constantius II. A second church, ordered by Theodosius II, was inaugurated on 10 October 415. It was destroyed, and on 23 February 532, only a few weeks later, Justinian began a third and entirely different basilica, larger and more majestic than its predecessors. He appointed two architects to design it, the mathematician Anthemius of Tralles and the geometer and engineer Isidore of Miletus.

The dome is carried on four spherical triangular pendentives, making the building one of the first large-scale uses of that element. It was the largest pendentive dome in the world until St Peter's Basilica, and its height is much lower than that of any other dome of such a diameter. After the vault first collapsed, the dome was rebuilt in 558. The church stayed the largest in the world for more than five hundred years, until the abbey church at Cluny was completed in the 12th century. The horseshoe-shaped upper gallery was reserved for the empress and her court. The Imperial Gate was originally used only by the emperor.

Under Justinian the interior had abstract designs on marble slabs and mosaics on the vaults, with a few figurative decorations. Figurative mosaics added later were destroyed during the iconoclastic controversy of 726–843, and the surviving mosaics are post-iconoclastic. The minarets are Ottoman additions, and the two western ones, by Selim II and designed by Mimar Sinan, are 60 metres high. Sinan also directed the building of buttresses, and 24 were added in all.

For nearly a thousand years Hagia Sophia was the religious centre of the Eastern Orthodox Church. In 1054 the envoy of Pope Leo IX, Humbert of Silva Candida, delivered the excommunication of Patriarch Michael I Cerularius there, an act considered the start of the East–West Schism. In 1204, during the Fourth Crusade, it became a Catholic cathedral under the Latin Empire, and it was restored to the Orthodox Church in 1261. Enrico Dandolo, the doge of Venice who led the Crusade, was buried in the church.

After Constantinople fell to the Ottoman Empire on 29 May 1453, Mehmed II performed the Friday prayer there and ordered its conversion to a mosque. It was the principal mosque of Istanbul until the Sultan Ahmed Mosque was built in 1616. Mustafa Kemal Atatürk made it a museum in 1935, and in 2020 it was reclassified as a mosque. Its style became the model for Eastern Orthodox church architecture and was emulated by Ottoman mosques, including the Şehzade Mosque and the Süleymaniye Mosque.
haifa: Haifa lies on the Israeli Mediterranean coastal plain, at the mouth of the Kishon River and on the northern slopes of Mount Carmel around Haifa Bay. The city is split over three tiers: the lowest holds commerce, industry and the port, the middle level the older residential districts, and the upper level modern neighbourhoods. It is about 90 km north of Tel Aviv. The origin of its name is unclear; proposals include the high priest Caiaphas, a Hebrew root meaning to cover or shield, and the Hebrew words for 'beautiful shore'.

The earliest known settlement nearby was Tell Abu Hawam, a port and fishing village founded in the Late Bronze Age, in the fourteenth century BCE. Haifa is first mentioned in Talmudic literature about the third century CE, as a Jewish fishing village whose fishermen caught murex snails for purple dye. After the Arab conquest of the Levant it was overshadowed by the port of Akka.

Shortly after the First Crusade the crusaders took Haifa after a fierce battle with its Jewish inhabitants and Fatimid garrison, and it became a small fortified stronghold in the Principality of Galilee. Saladin's army captured it in July 1187 after the Battle of Hattin, and the crusaders under Richard the Lionheart retook it in 1191. In the 1760s the old settlement was moved 2.5 km east as a fortified town, today the Old City.

British forces captured Haifa in September 1918. Its population was 98 percent Arab in 1872, and Jewish immigration from 1881 changed the balance, so that by 1945 it was 55 percent Jewish and 45 percent Arab. During and after the Battle of Haifa in the 1948 war most of the Arab population fled or was expelled, and the Old City was later demolished.

Haifa is the third-largest city in Israel, with 297,082 inhabitants in 2024. The Baháʼí World Centre, a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a destination for Baháʼí pilgrimage, stands there. The city has a major seaport, the Technion and the University of Haifa, and the Carmelit underground railway. About ten percent of the population is Arab.
hainan: Hainan consists of Hainan Island and more than 200 smaller islands in the South China Sea. Its name literally means South of the Sea, after its position south of the Qiongzhou Strait, a channel 20 kilometres wide that separates it from the Leizhou Peninsula of Guangdong. The province has a land area of 33,920 square kilometres, almost all of it the island, which is slightly smaller than Taiwan. Wuzhi Mountain, at 1,840 metres, is the highest peak. The climate is mostly tropical, and the island holds over 1,500 square kilometres of tropical forest. Earlier names for the island include Zhuya, Qiongya and Qiongzhou.

Hainan Island was recorded by Chinese officials in 110 BCE, when the Western Han dynasty established a military garrison there after the arrival of General Lu Bode. Over many centuries imperial authorities exiled people condemned as criminals or political dissidents to Hainan and northern Vietnam, where banished people were put to harsh labour in the tropical climate. The Hlai, a Kra-Dai-speaking people, are native to the island.

After 1912 Hainan was organised as the Qiongya Circuit within Guangdong, and in 1920 Sun Yat-sen proposed a Qiongya Special District. The Hainan Special Administrative District was formally established in 1949. On 1 May 1950, under the People's Republic of China, it became an Administrative Region Office, a branch of the Guangdong provincial government. On 13 April 1988 the National People's Congress decided to establish Hainan Province, and Deng Xiaoping's reform and opening up programme made it a special economic zone.

The capital is Haikou on the northern coast, and Sanya on the southern coast is a well-known tourist destination. Han Chinese make up 82% of the population and the Hlai 15%. Most people speak Hainanese, a variety of Min Chinese, and most practise Chinese folk religion and Chinese Buddhism.
haiti: Haiti forms the western three-eighths of Hispaniola, the second-largest island of the Greater Antilles, and shares a border of 360 km with the Dominican Republic. It is the most mountainous country in the Caribbean, with plains covering only 22% of its territory, and the highest point is Pic la Selle at 2,680 m. The name comes from the Taino language and means land of high mountains. It was the native name for the whole island, and Jean-Jacques Dessalines restored it as the official name of independent Saint-Domingue, in tribute to the Amerindian predecessors.

Indigenous peoples have lived on Hispaniola for about 6,000 years. Arawakan-speaking ancestors of the Taino arrived during the 1st millennium BCE, and at the time of European contact the island was divided among five caciquedoms led by chiefs. Christopher Columbus landed on 6 December 1492 and claimed the island for the Crown of Castile. The 39 men he left behind founded La Navidad but were later killed by the Taino.

European diseases caused epidemics among the native people, the first recorded smallpox epidemic in the Americas breaking out on Hispaniola in 1507, and the encomienda system, which forced natives to work in gold mines and plantations, reduced their numbers further. Spain held the island until 1697, when the western part was ceded to France as Saint-Domingue, a plantation colony worked by enslaved Africans.

The Haitian Revolution of 1791 to 1804 made Haiti the first sovereign state in the Caribbean and the first country in the Americas to abolish slavery officially. The independent state began as an empire, later split into two and reunited in 1820, and a second empire under Faustin Soulouque ended with the return of the republic in 1859. The 19th century brought instability, international isolation and a crippling debt to France. United States forces occupied Haiti from 1915 to 1934, and the Duvalier family ruled as dictators from 1957 to 1986.

Haiti is a republic with Port-au-Prince as its capital and largest city, and about 11 million people, the most in the Caribbean. Its culture blends French and African customs with Spanish and Indigenous influences. The Citadelle Laferrière, built between 1805 and 1820, and the Sans-Souci Palace were inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 1982.
hajj: The word ḥajj is similar to the Hebrew ḥag, 'festival', from the same Semitic root; the Hebrew term referred to the three pilgrimage festivals Israelites made to the Temple in Jerusalem each year. The present pattern of Hajj was established by Muhammad, but according to the Quran, elements of it trace back to Abraham. In Islamic tradition Abraham left his wife Hajar and his son Ishmael in the desert of ancient Mecca. Hajar ran seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwah looking for water, and a spring then rose beneath Ishmael's foot. Abraham was later commanded to build the Kaaba with Ishmael's help and to invite people to make pilgrimage there. The Quran refers to these events in verses 2:124–127 and 22:27–30.

Hajj is an annual pilgrimage to Mecca and one of the Five Pillars of Islam. It is a once-in-a-lifetime duty for every Muslim who is physically and financially able to make the journey and to support their family during their absence. Its rites are carried out over five to six days, from the 8th to the 12th or 13th of Dhu'l-Hijja, the last month of the Islamic calendar. Because that calendar is lunar, the Gregorian date moves each year, and the season falls twice in one Gregorian year about every 33 years.

The pilgrim enters the sacred state of ihram, wearing unstitched white clothing, and walks seven times counterclockwise around the Kaaba, an act called tawaf, then walks seven times between Safa and Marwah. On 9 Dhu'l-Hijja, the Day of Arafah, pilgrims stand in vigil on the plain of Arafat, about 20 km east of Mecca, from noon until sunset; a pilgrim's Hajj is considered invalid without this. They spend a night at Muzdalifah, and on 10 Dhu'l-Hijja at Mina they throw seven stones at the largest of three pillars representing Satan.

After the sacrifice of an animal, pilgrims shave or trim their hair, and the festival of Eid al-Adha follows. The shorter pilgrimage to Mecca, Umrah, can be made at other times of the year but does not replace the Hajj.
hamburg: Hamburg lies at a sheltered natural harbour on the southern fanning-out of the Jutland Peninsula, between continental Europe to the south and Scandinavia to the north, with the North Sea to the west and the Baltic Sea to the northeast. It stands on the River Elbe at its confluence with the Alster and Bille, where the 110 km Elbe estuary begins. The city centre is around the Binnenalster and Außenalster, both lakes formed by damming the Alster. The Altes Land, part of the city, is the largest contiguous fruit-producing region in Central Europe.

Claudius Ptolemy, in the 2nd century CE, reported the first name for the vicinity as Treva. The name Hamburg comes from the first permanent building on the site, a castle which Charlemagne ordered built in 808. It rose on rocky terrain in a marsh between the Alster and the Elbe as a defence against Slavic incursion and acquired the name Hammaburg, burg meaning castle or fort.

In 834 Hamburg became the seat of a bishopric, whose first bishop, Ansgar, later known as the Apostle of the North, founded the city's early Christian institutions. Two years later it was linked with Bremen to form the Bishopric of Hamburg-Bremen. The town was destroyed repeatedly in its early centuries. In 845 a fleet of 600 Viking ships sailed up the Elbe and destroyed it, when it had about 500 inhabitants. King Mieszko II Lambert of Poland burned it in 1030, and Valdemar II of Denmark raided and occupied it in 1201 and 1214. The Black Death reached Hamburg in 1350 and killed at least 60 per cent of its population, and the city suffered several major fires in the medieval period.

Hamburg was a member of the Hanseatic League and a free imperial city of the Holy Roman Empire. Before the unification of Germany in 1871 it was a fully sovereign city state, and before 1919 it was a civic republic headed constitutionally by a class of hereditary Grand Burghers, or Hanseaten. Later disasters included the Great Fire of 1842, the Allied fire-bombing of 1943 and the North Sea flood of 1962.

Officially the Free and Hanseatic City of Hamburg, it is the second-largest city in Germany after Berlin and one of the country's three city-states, with Berlin and Bremen. Its population is over 1.9 million. The Port of Hamburg is Germany's largest. The Speicherstadt and Kontorhausviertel were declared World Heritage Sites by UNESCO in 2015.
han-dynasty: The Han dynasty was established by Liu Bang after the short-lived Qin dynasty collapsed within four years of the death of Qin Shi Huang. Two former rebel leaders, Xiang Yu of Chu and Liu Bang of Han, fought for hegemony, and Liu Bang defeated Xiang Yu at the Battle of Gaixia in 202 BCE. He took the title of emperor and is known after death as Emperor Gaozu. Chang'an, modern Xi'an, became the capital. The dynasty took its name from Hanzhong, the small fief on the Han River that Xiang Yu had given Liu Bang. The Western Han lasted until 9 CE, and the Eastern Han formally began on 5 August 25 CE, when Liu Xiu became Emperor Guangwu.

The Xiongnu defeated the Han in 200 BCE, and the court responded with marriage alliances and payments of tribute. Emperor Wu changed this policy in 133 BCE with a series of campaigns that took the Hexi Corridor and the Tarim Basin from the Xiongnu, helping to establish the Silk Road. He also annexed Nanyue in 111 BCE and Dian in 109 BCE, and in 108 BCE Han forces conquered Gojoseon and set up the Xuantu and Lelang commanderies in Korea. From his reign onward the court sponsored Confucianism, and in 124 BCE he established the Imperial University. To finance his campaigns he nationalised the salt and iron industries in 117 BCE, monopolies repealed under the Eastern Han.

Wang Mang, regent after the death of Emperor Ai, interrupted the dynasty with his Xin dynasty from 9 to 23 CE. After 92 CE palace eunuchs became involved in violent power struggles with the consort clans of the empresses. The Yellow Turban and Five Pecks of Rice rebellions, led by Taoist religious societies, challenged imperial authority in 184. After the death of Emperor Ling in 189 the eunuchs were massacred by military officers, and governors became warlords who divided the empire. The dynasty ended in 220 when Cao Pi, king of Wei, usurped the throne from Emperor Xian.

The emperor stood at the apex of society and was in theory unlimited in power, but ministers pressed him through institutions such as the court conference, and emperors were often minors ruled over by a regent. Below him came the kings of the Liu clan, and the empire was divided into provinces, commanderies and counties, plus semi-autonomous kingdoms that lost autonomy after the Rebellion of the Seven States. Taxes were paid in coin, and the poll tax stimulated a money economy. Han technology included papermaking, which the Han tradition credits to Cai Lun in 105, rudders, raised-relief maps and seismometers. Today the majority ethnic group of China calls itself the Han people.
hangul: Before Hangul, Korea had used Hanja, Chinese characters, since antiquity. The script was difficult, which limited its use mostly to the upper class and left commoners largely illiterate, and it was poorly suited to a language not closely related to Chinese: Korean pronunciation and ideas could be represented only indirectly. The Joseon king Sejong the Great, who reigned from 1418 to 1450, was responsible for Hangul's creation, and most scholars believe he was personally and significantly involved.

Because records are lacking, it is unknown when work began or what the process was. The script was first introduced, probably in a mostly complete form, to Sejong's court in the 12th month of 1443 of the Korean calendar, roughly 30 December 1443 to 28 January 1444. It was officially published in 1446 in the text Hunminjeongeum and its companion commentary, the Haerye. Part of the effort that followed produced the Yongbiŏch'ŏn'ga, the first work of Hangul literature.

The original name, Hunminjeongeum, means 'Correct Sounds for the Instruction of the People'. Modern Korean orthographies use 24 basic letters, called jamo: 14 consonants and 10 vowels. Combinations bring the total to 51. The letters are arranged in syllable blocks made of an initial consonant, a vowel and an optional final consonant. Linguists classify the script as a phonographic alphabet, and some have called it a featural script, one in which letter shapes encode features of speech.

The letters were designed to be graphically simple, traditionally of only straight lines, dots and circles. The shapes of five basic consonants are based on those of the human speech organs, and most of the other basic consonants are derived from them by adding lines to show progressively harsher sounds.

Sejong tried to spread Hangul through government and society with limited success. In the 15th century it was rarely used, mainly in Seoul among people close to the court, and it began to spread beyond Seoul in the 16th century. Women and Buddhists were significant early adopters, and women often taught it at home, though it was rarely taught in Confucian curricula. The elite looked down on it for centuries.

After Korea ended its isolation in the 1870s the script came to be seen as a symbol of national identity, and reform movements, together called the Hangul Movement, arose. Under Japanese colonial rule from 1910 its use was repressed to varying degrees, and it expanded after the 1919 March First Movement. After 1945 usage diverged in the two Koreas; North Korea's Compendium of Korean Language Norms appeared in 1966 and South Korea's Hangeul Orthography in 1989. Hangul is now the predominant script for Korean.
hangzhou: Hangzhou lies in northwestern Zhejiang province, at the southern end of the Grand Canal, which runs to Beijing, in the south-central part of the Yangtze River Delta. The city centre is built around the eastern and northern sides of West Lake, just north of the Qiantang River, the largest river in Zhejiang. Each year a tidal bore races up the Qiantang through Hangzhou, reaching up to 12 m in height. The climate is humid subtropical, with long, hot, humid summers and chilly, drier winters.

The Hemudu culture inhabited Yuyao, 100 km south-east of Hangzhou, as far back as seven thousand years ago, when rice was first cultivated in southeast China. The jade-carving Liangzhu culture, named for its type site just northwest of the city, lived in the surrounding area around five thousand years ago. Hangzhou was established as a county seat in 221 BCE and later served as the capital of the Wuyue Kingdom (923 to 997).

Under the Tang dynasty the poet Bai Juyi, as governor, had a stronger and taller dyke built to hold the water of West Lake, which the surrounding farmland depended on, and had willows planted along it. In 1089 another poet-governor, Su Shi, used 200,000 workers to build a 2.8 km causeway across the lake from mud dredged from its bottom.

Hangzhou became the capital of the Southern Song dynasty after the Jurchens conquered most of northern China and captured Kaifeng in the Jingkang Incident of 1127. The surviving imperial family had retreated south, and Emperor Gaozong moved from Nanjing to Shangqiu to Yangzhou before settling at Hangzhou. The city was besieged and captured by the Mongol armies of Kublai Khan in 1276. The historian Patricia Buckley Ebrey noted that the Mongols spared Hangzhou and the Zhao royal family of the Southern Song, while they had killed the Jurchen Wanyan royal family by the hundreds at the Siege of Kaifeng in 1232. The new Yuan capital was Dadu (Beijing), but Hangzhou remained an important commercial and administrative centre for the south.

The port remained important until the middle of the Ming dynasty, when its harbour slowly silted up. Under the Qing it held an imperial army garrison. The Taiping Heavenly Kingdom occupied the city in 1856 and 1860, and it was heavily damaged in its conquest, occupation and reconquest by the Qing army.

Hangzhou is the capital and most populous city of Zhejiang province and a sub-provincial city. Three UNESCO World Heritage Sites lie in or near it: the West Lake Cultural Landscape, the Grand Canal and the Archaeological Ruins of Liangzhu City. Its native residents speak the Hangzhou dialect, a Wu dialect, and its cuisine is regarded as representative of Zhejiang cooking.
hannibal: Hannibal was one of the sons of the Carthaginian general and statesman Hamilcar Barca and an unknown mother, and was most likely born in Carthage. His name combines the name Hanno with the god Baal Hammon, and its exact vocalisation is debated. He had two brothers, Hasdrubal and Mago. His brothers-in-law, Hasdrubal the Fair and the Numidian king Naravas, were close associates of his father in the Mercenary War and the Punic conquest of the Iberian Peninsula. Rome's defeat of Carthage in the First Punic War had left deep tension, and Hannibal pledged to his father never to be a friend of Rome.

In 218 BCE Hannibal attacked Saguntum, an ally of Rome in Hispania, which sparked the Second Punic War. He invaded Italy by way of the Alps with North African war elephants, and about 10,000 Celtic tribesmen joined his army in the Po Valley. He won victories at Ticinus, Trebia, Lake Trasimene and Cannae. At Cannae in 216 BCE he seized the supply depot on the Apulian plain; the Roman army there is estimated by some at 100,000 but more likely 50,000 to 80,000.

The war then settled into a stalemate. Following the strategy of Fabius Maximus, called Cunctator, the Romans refused open battle and wore down Hannibal's army with smaller forces. Carthaginian defeats in Hispania prevented his reinforcement, and he held most of southern Italy for about 15 years without a decisive victory.

In 203 BCE a Roman invasion of North Africa under Scipio Africanus led to his recall to Carthage. At the Battle of Zama in 202 BCE the Romans had the superior cavalry, after King Masinissa of Numidia changed sides, while the Carthaginians had more infantry and 80 elephants. Hannibal was defeated, ending the war.

After the peace left Carthage with an indemnity of ten thousand talents, Hannibal was elected suffete, or chief magistrate. He reorganised the state's finances to end corruption and recover embezzled funds so that the indemnity could be paid without raising taxes. The reforms were unpopular with members of the Carthaginian aristocracy and in Rome, and he went into voluntary exile.

He served as a military adviser to Antiochus III the Great at the Seleucid court in his war with Rome. After Antiochus lost at the Battle of Magnesia, Hannibal fled again, stopping in Armenia and reaching the court of Bithynia. There he was betrayed to the Romans and died by suicide, poisoning himself.
hanoi: Hanoi lies on the Red River, whose curved course around the city was symbolised as a dragon. Several of the city's older names contain the Chinese word for dragon: it was first called Long Biên, then Tống Bình and Long Đỗ, and after its recapture in 866 by the Tang general Gao Pian it was renamed Đại La. Medieval Muslim sources between the 9th and 12th century called it Luqin, a term derived from Longbian.

Stone tools of the Sơn Vi culture, 10,000 to 20,000 years old, have been found at Ba Vì and Đông Anh. From about 10,000 to 4,000 years ago the area was under water as the sea rose, and the region is believed to have been inhabited continuously for the last 4,000 years.

Around the third century BCE a fortified citadel, later named Cổ Loa, was built in the area; it was the first political centre of the Vietnamese civilisation before Chinese influence, with an outer embankment covering 600 hectares. In 179 BCE Nanyue annexed the region, and Zhao Tuo left the indigenous chiefs in control of the population. For the first time the area formed part of a polity headed by a Chinese ruler.

In 1010, under the Lý dynasty, Emperor Lý Thái Tổ established the capital of Đại Việt in what later became central Hanoi and named it Thăng Long, meaning ascending dragon. In 1428 King Lê Lợi renamed it Đông Kinh, eastern capital, a name used until 1789. In 1802 the Nguyễn dynasty moved the national capital to Huế, and the city was renamed Hanoi in 1831. The French took control in 1888 and shaped the city's architecture to their tastes. Hanoi was the capital of the French protectorate of Tonkin from 1883 to 1949 and of French Indochina from 1902 to 1945. Ernest Hebrard drew up a development plan in 1924, which was partly carried out.

After the August Revolution and the fall of the Nguyễn dynasty, the Democratic Republic of Vietnam made Hanoi its capital. The city was part of the State of Vietnam from 1949 to 1954 and again of the Democratic Republic from 1954 to 1976. In 1976 it became the capital of the unified Socialist Republic of Vietnam.

Hanoi is the capital and second most populous centrally governed city of Vietnam, with about 8.7 million people. Its Old Quarter, near Hoàn Kiếm Lake, keeps most of its original street layout, descended from the 36 streets where merchants specialised in trades such as silk, jewellery or bamboo. The city also holds the Imperial Citadel of Thăng Long, the Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum and the French colonial Hanoi Opera House and St. Joseph's Cathedral. UNESCO gave Hanoi the title City for Peace on 16 July 1999.
hanover: Hanover lies at the confluence of the River Leine and its tributary the Ihme, in the south of the North German Plain and northwest of the Harz mountains. Its position at a natural crossroads and on the upper navigable reaches of the Leine shaped its growth. The river linked it to the Hanseatic League city of Bremen, and east-west traffic skirting the Harz between the Low Countries and Saxony or Thuringia passed through it.

Hanover was founded in medieval times on the east bank of the Leine. Its original name, Honovere, may mean high river bank, though this is debated. A small village of ferrymen and fishermen, it became a comparatively large town in the 13th century and received town privileges in 1241. It was the capital of the Principality of Calenberg from 1636 to 1692 and of the Electorate of Hanover from 1692 to 1814. From 1714 to 1837 it was by personal union the family seat of the Hanoverian kings of Great Britain and Ireland.

In July 1803 Napoleon imposed the Convention of Artlenburg, and about 35,000 French soldiers occupied the country. George III did not recognise the convention, and many Hanoverian soldiers emigrated to Britain, where the King's German Legion was formed; it later played a part in the Peninsular War and at Waterloo in 1815. The electorate became the Kingdom of Hanover in 1814. After 1866 Hanover was the capital of a province of Prussia, and the city passed 100,000 inhabitants in 1875. It lay in the British zone of occupation after the Second World War and became part of the new state of Lower Saxony in 1946.

Hanover is the capital and largest city of Lower Saxony, with a population of 535,932 in 2021. It is a major crossing of railway lines and motorways and one of the world's leading exhibition cities; its fairground, extended especially for Expo 2000, is the largest in the world, and the Hanover Fair has been held since 1947. The Great Garden of the Royal Gardens of Herrenhausen is an important European Baroque garden. The palace there was largely destroyed by Allied bombing and reopened after reconstruction in 2013.
hans-christian-andersen: Hans Christian Andersen was born in Odense on 2 April 1805. His father, also named Hans, had an elementary school education and introduced his son to literature by reading him the Arabian Nights; his mother, Anne Marie Andersdatter, was an illiterate washerwoman. After his father's death in 1816 the boy attended a local school for poor children and had to support himself, working as an apprentice to a weaver and later to a tailor.

At 14 he moved to Copenhagen to seek work as an actor and was accepted into the Royal Danish Theatre for his soprano voice, which soon broke. A colleague told him he considered him a poet, and Andersen turned to writing. Jonas Collin, the theatre's director, persuaded King Frederick VI to pay part of his schooling at Slagelse and later Elsinore, which lasted until 1827.

His first story, "The Ghost at Palnatoke's Grave", appeared in 1822. In 1829 he had considerable success with the short story "A Journey on Foot from Holmen's Canal to the East Point of Amager", followed by a play and a short volume of poems. A small travel grant from the king in 1833 let him begin the first of many journeys through Europe, and he reached Rome in October 1834. His travels in Italy shaped his first novel, The Improvisatore, a fictionalized autobiography published in 1835 to instant acclaim.

Andersen's first fairy tales were issued in three booklets by C. A. Reitzel in Copenhagen between May 1835 and April 1837. The first, of 8 May 1835, held "The Tinderbox", "Little Claus and Big Claus", "The Princess and the Pea" and "Little Ida's Flowers"; the first three were based on folktales he had heard in childhood. In June 1847 he visited England and met Charles Dickens. In 1857 he stayed five weeks at Dickens's home, Gads Hill Place, after which Dickens stopped writing to him, which Andersen never understood.

In early 1872 Andersen fell out of his bed and was severely hurt, and soon afterwards he showed signs of liver cancer. He died on 4 August 1875 at Rolighed, a country house near Copenhagen belonging to his friends Moritz G. Melchior and his wife. By then he was internationally revered, and the Danish government paid him an annual stipend as a national treasure. His 156 fairy tales in nine volumes have been translated into more than 125 languages and have inspired ballets, plays and films.
harare: Harare lies in north-eastern Zimbabwe, in the Mashonaland region, on one of the higher parts of the Highveld plateau at an elevation of 1,483 metres. Its climate is subtropical highland, cooler and drier than a tropical or subtropical climate because of the altitude and a cool south-easterly airflow. The original landscape could be described as parkland, and Harare Kopje, at 1,540 metres, is the highest point in the city. The name comes from the village near Harare Kopje of the Shona chief Neharawa, whose nickname was he who does not sleep.

The Pioneer Column, a military volunteer force of settlers organised by Cecil Rhodes for the British South Africa Company, founded the city as a fort on 12 September 1890. It was named Fort Salisbury after the British prime minister, the 3rd Marquess of Salisbury, and became known simply as Salisbury. Company administrators demarcated the city and ran it until Southern Rhodesia achieved responsible government in 1923. Salisbury was declared a municipality in 1897 and became a city in 1935.

After the Second World War the city expanded rapidly with its designation as capital of the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland from 1953 to 1963, with significant immigration from Great Britain, Southern Africa and, to a lesser extent, Southern Europe. Suburbs such as Alexandra Park and Mount Pleasant sprawled outwards as motor vehicle ownership grew, while mostly black suburbs like Highfield suffered from overcrowding. The Federation was dissolved in 1963. Ian Smith's Rhodesian Front government declared Rhodesia independent of the United Kingdom on 11 November 1965 and kept Salisbury as the capital, and the country was internationally recognised as independent under the name Zimbabwe on 18 April 1980.

The city was renamed Harare on 18 April 1982, the second anniversary of independence. Before the change the black residential area now called Mbare was known as Harari. Investment in education and healthcare produced a growing middle class, and the Eastgate Centre and the New Reserve Bank Tower became landmarks of the period.

Harare is the capital and largest city of Zimbabwe, with 1,849,600 inhabitants in the 2022 census and an estimated 2,487,209 in its metropolitan province, which also includes Chitungwiza, Epworth and Ruwa. It is the country's financial, commercial and communications centre and a trading centre for tobacco, maize, cotton and citrus fruits. About 90 percent of its people are Shona-speaking. The University of Zimbabwe, founded in 1952, is in the city, and the National Gallery, the National Archives and the Harare Gardens stand in its central district. The city hosted the 1995 All-Africa Games and the 2003 Cricket World Cup.
harbin: Harbin lies in southern Heilongjiang on the south bank of the middle Songhua River, at the south-eastern edge of the Songnen Plain. The terrain is generally flat and low. It is the northernmost of China's major cities and has long, dry and freezing winters, which have earned it the nickname Ice City. The city government says the name means 'swan' in Jurchen, while other sources derive it from a Manchu word meaning 'a place for drying fishing nets'.

Human settlement in the area dates from at least 2200 BCE. Wanyan Aguda, founder of the Jin dynasty, who reigned from 1115 to 1123, came from the Jurchen Wanyan tribes living near the Ashi River. In 1115 he established the Jin capital, Shangjing Huiningfu, in what is now Acheng District of Harbin. Wanyan Liang moved the capital to Yanjing, now Beijing, in 1153, and Wanyan Yong restored the city as a secondary capital in 1173.

The modern city dates from 1898, when the Russian Empire built the Chinese Eastern Railway. The Polish engineer Adam Szydłowski drew plans for the city, and the Russians made it the base of their administration of the railway. The settlement grew into a city within five years, with settlers from across the Russian Empire, including Ukrainians, Poles, Jews, Georgians and Tatars. In the 1920s it was considered China's fashion capital.

Japan invaded Manchuria after the Mukden Incident of September 1931, and Japanese forces occupied Harbin within hours. From 1932 until 1945 it was the largest city of the puppet state of Manchukuo. The Soviet Army took the city on 20 August 1945 and handed it to the People's Liberation Army in April 1946. Most of the European community left in the early 1950s, so that by 1964 the Russian population was reduced to 450.

Harbin is the capital and largest city of Heilongjiang, with a metropolitan population of 10,009,854 at the 2020 census. Its Russian and European legacy survives in Central Street and in Saint Sophia Cathedral. UNESCO named Harbin a City of Music in 2010, and the city is known for its winter ice sculpture festival.
harry-s-truman: Harry S. Truman was born in Lamar, Missouri, on 8 May 1884, the oldest child of John Anderson Truman and Martha Ellen Young Truman. His middle initial honours both his grandfathers and is not an abbreviation of one name. His father was a farmer and livestock dealer, and the family settled in Independence, Missouri, when Harry was six. He was refused an appointment to West Point because of poor eyesight and served in the Missouri National Guard from 1905 to 1911.

When the United States entered World War I on 6 April 1917, Truman rejoined his battery and fought in France as a captain in the Field Artillery. In 1919 he married Bess Wallace. He and Edward Jacobson opened a haberdashery in Kansas City, which went bankrupt in the recession of 1921.

Truman was elected a judge of Jackson County in 1922 and a senator for Missouri in 1934. From 1940 to 1944 he gained national prominence as chairman of the Truman Committee, which aimed to reduce waste and inefficiency in wartime contracts. He was nominated as Franklin D. Roosevelt's running mate, though reluctant, and was sworn in as vice president on 20 January 1945. He became president on Roosevelt's death in April. Only then was he told about the Manhattan Project and the atomic bomb.

As president Truman authorized the use of nuclear weapons against the Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, set up the Marshall Plan and established the Truman Doctrine. He supported the founding of NATO and presided over the onset of the Cold War in 1947 and the Berlin Airlift in 1948. When Congress refused his proposal for comprehensive civil rights legislation, he issued orders that prohibited discrimination in federal agencies and desegregated the armed forces. He won the 1948 election against Thomas E. Dewey. The Korean War lasted from 1950 to 1953. Corruption in parts of his administration, which did not implicate Truman himself, became a campaign issue in 1952, and he chose not to run again.

In retirement Truman founded his presidential library and published his memoirs. He was admitted to hospital in Kansas City with pneumonia on 5 December 1972, developed multiple organ failure and died on 26 December, aged 88. When he left office in 1953 his administration was heavily criticised, but public feeling towards him grew warmer over the following decades.
harsha-of-kashmir: Harsha, also called Harshadeva, was born in 1059, the son of King Kalasha of Kashmir. Almost everything known of him comes from the Rajatarangini of Kalhana, whose father Champaka had been one of Harsha's ministers and who wrote in the time of Jayasimha, between 1127 and 1159. According to Kalhana he was built like a god and extremely handsome. He is said to have begun as a capable and noble king before his spending brought him into financial trouble.

Extravagant outlay on his troops and on pleasures left the king in grave difficulties. The historian Prithvi Nath Kaul Bamzai notes Kalhana's statement that even night soil was taxed. An accidental discovery of hoarded treasure at the Bhimasahi temple led him to despoil other temples and to melt down gold and silver images. Kalhana writes that not one temple kept its images, and that only two chief divine images were respected, Ranaswamin in the city and Martanda. Two colossal statues of the Buddha were saved by requests made one at Parihasapura by the singer Kanaka and one in the city by the monk Kusalsri.

Kalhana calls him that Turushka, and he bore the epithet raja-Turushka, Turk king. Turkish troops served him as mercenaries, and the chronicle says he continually supported Turushka captains-of-hundreds with money, while adding that he ate domesticated pigs until his death. According to the historian André Wink, Harsha in all likelihood took up the Muslim tradition of iconoclasm, as the epithet indicates. Kalhana also charges him with credulity towards parasites at court, who passed off slave girls as goddesses, and with incest with his sisters and violence against Naga, his father's sister's daughter.

Harsha died on 31 August 1101, the last ruler of the First Lohara dynasty. His conduct has remained a subject of discussion. The great Buddha of the capital outlived him: Kalhana records that when a fire reduced the city to a heap of earth in the reign of Sussala, the statue alone stood visible, blackened by smoke. The statue at Parihasapura had been made by Lalitaditya Muktapida, and Abul-Fazl states that the temples of that place were finally destroyed by Sikandar Butshikan, who ruled from 1389 to 1413.
hartford-connecticut: Hartford lies on the west bank of the Connecticut River, which forms the boundary between Hartford and East Hartford. The city covers about 47 square kilometres, of which about 1.8 square kilometres is water. It is bordered by the towns of West Hartford, Newington, Wethersfield, East Hartford, Bloomfield, South Windsor, Glastonbury and Windsor. Several Algonquian peoples lived in or around the area, including the Podunks east of the river, the Poquonocks, the Massacoes, the Tunxis, the Wangunks, and the Saukiog in Hartford itself.

The first Europeans known to have explored the area were the Dutch under Adriaen Block, who sailed up the Connecticut River in 1614. Dutch fur traders from New Amsterdam returned in 1623 to establish a trading post for the Dutch West India Company, partly to control the flow of wampum, the de facto currency of New Netherland and parts of New England. Their fort, Fort Hoop or the House of Hope, stood on the south bank of the Park River. In 1633 Jacob Van Curler formally bought the land around it from the Pequot chief. The fort was abandoned by 1654, and the area is still called Dutch Point.

Hartford alternated with New Haven as dual capital of Connecticut from 1664 and has been the sole capital since 1875. On 15 December 1814 delegates from the five New England states met at the Hartford Convention to discuss New England's possible secession from the United States. In the early nineteenth century the area was a centre of abolitionist activity, notably through the Beecher family: the minister Lyman Beecher, his daughter Harriet Beecher Stowe, author of Uncle Tom's Cabin, and Isabella Beecher Hooker, a leading figure in the women's rights movement. The American School for the Deaf, founded by Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet in 1817, was the first school for deaf children in the country.

After the American Civil War Hartford was the richest city in the United States for several decades. The Connecticut River reached a record flood stage in April 1909. On 6 July 1944 a fire at a performance of the Ringling Brothers and Barnum and Bailey Circus, known as the Hartford Circus Fire, killed 168 people, mostly children and their mothers.

Hartford is the capital of Connecticut and the core of the Greater Hartford metropolitan area, which has about 1.17 million residents. The city itself had a population of 121,054 at the 2020 census. It is nicknamed the Insurance Capital of the World, and the industry remains the region's largest. The city holds the Wadsworth Atheneum, the oldest continuously operating public art museum in the country, Bushnell Park, and the Mark Twain House, where Mark Twain wrote his best-known works. The Hartford Courant, founded in 1764, is the oldest continuously published newspaper in the United States.
harvard-university: Harvard was founded and authorised by the Great and General Court of the Massachusetts Bay Colony. Its first headmaster, Nathaniel Eaton, took office the following year, and in 1638 the college acquired English North America's first known printing press. In the same year John Harvard, a Puritan clergyman who had emigrated from England, bequeathed it £780 and his library of some 320 volumes, and the college was named in his honour. Its earliest known official seal, of 1650, bears the motto In Christi Gloriam, To the glory of Christ. Although never formally affiliated with any Protestant denomination, Harvard trained Congregational clergy until its curriculum and student body were gradually secularised in the 18th century.

Harvard faculty and students largely supported the Patriot cause in the American Revolution. The Constitution of Massachusetts recognised the college as a university in 1780. In the 19th century Enlightenment ideas of reason and free will, widespread among Congregational ministers, set liberals against more traditional Calvinist pastors. The election of Henry Ware as Hollis professor of divinity in 1805 and the appointment of the liberal Samuel Webber as president in 1807 marked a shift to more liberal and Arminian ideas.

Under President Charles William Eliot, who served from 1869 to 1909, Harvard developed several professional schools and became a modern research university. Eliot, a chemist who had studied two years in Germany, used the German model: a graduate department formed in 1872 granted its first PhD degrees in 1873. Harvard Law School was established in 1817 through a bequest of 1779 by Isaac Royall Jr., and Harvard Business School in 1908. In 1900 Harvard became a founding member of the Association of American Universities, and James B. Conant led it through the Great Depression and the Second World War.

Harvard Yard in Cambridge, Massachusetts, holds Massachusetts Hall, built between 1718 and 1720 and the oldest building still standing. The university has three campuses, in Cambridge, in Allston and in Boston's Longwood Medical Area. Harvard Library, centred on Widener Library, holds more than 20 million volumes. The Harvard Crimson student newspaper, founded in 1873, counts among its alumni the presidents Franklin D. Roosevelt and John F. Kennedy.
haryana: Haryana is a landlocked state in north-western India. It is bordered by Punjab and Himachal Pradesh to the north, Rajasthan to the west and south and Delhi to the south-east, while the Yamuna forms its eastern boundary with Uttar Pradesh. Most of it lies on the fertile Ghaggar Plain, part of the Indo-Gangetic Plain, and its highest point is Karoh Peak, 1,467 metres, in the Sivalik Hills. Some anthropologists believe the name comes from the period after the Mahabharata, when the Abhiras are thought to have settled there and developed advanced agricultural techniques.

The villages of Rakhigarhi in Hisar district and Bhirrana in Fatehabad district hold ancient sites of the Indus Valley Civilisation, with evidence of paved roads, drainage, terracotta brick and skilled metalworking. In the seventh century the Pushyabhuti dynasty ruled parts of northern India from Thanesar, and Harsha was its prominent king. The Tomara dynasty ruled the south of the region in the tenth century. In the British period the area was part of the province of Punjab, with princely states such as Jind, Kalsia, Loharu and Pataudi.

At the Partition of India, Punjab was divided between India and Pakistan, and Haryana became part of East Punjab. A significant number of Muslims left for Pakistan, and a huge number of Hindu and Sikh refugees arrived from West Punjab. The modern state was formed on 1 November 1966 under the Punjab Reorganisation Act. The Shah Commission, set up in April 1966, fixed the boundaries by the languages people spoke. Haryana took the predominantly Hindi-speaking south of the former Punjab, while Punjab kept the area where Punjabi speakers formed the majority.

The capital is Chandigarh, shared with Punjab. Gurgaon is among India's large financial and technology centres, and Faridabad is the most populous city. The state surrounds Delhi on three sides, so a large part of it lies within the National Capital Region. Hindi is the official language, and Punjabi has been a second official language since 2010. The 2011 census counted 25,351,462 people.
havana: Havana lies on the northern coast of Cuba along the Straits of Florida, south of the Florida Keys, where the Gulf of Mexico joins the Atlantic Ocean. The city extends mostly westward and southward from a bay, which is entered through a narrow inlet and divides into three main harbours. The Almendares River crosses the city from south to north.

The city stands mostly on low hills. A limestone ridge about 60 metres high slopes up from the east and culminates in the heights of La Cabaña and El Morro, where the Spanish built fortifications overlooking the eastern bay.

In the early 16th century Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar founded the town of San Cristóbal de la Habana on the southern coast of Cuba, at the mouth of the Mayabeque River, now the town of Batabanó. The low and swampy land caused the settlement to fail. In those years the Spanish established settlements on the northern coast, among them La Chorrera, at the mouth of the Almendares River. The town that became Havana grew up beside Puerto de Carenas, the Careening Port, in 1519, and the quality of the harbour led to the change of location.

Havana overtook Santiago in the mid-16th century because of the advantages of its harbour and became the capital of the island. It became a fundamental place for the Spanish colonial empire in the Americas and a stopping point for galleons returning to the Iberian Peninsula, and walls and forts were built to protect it from naval attacks. After the Cuban War of Independence a new constitution was adopted in 1901.

Havana is the capital and largest city of Cuba and the seat of its government. It is the country's main port. The population in 2021 was 2,142,939. Its economy first developed on its location as one of the early great trade centres of the New World, and sugar and a slave trade first brought riches to the city.

Old Havana, Habana Vieja, contains the core of the original city and was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982. Its landmarks include the Fortress San Carlos de la Cabaña, El Morro Castle, built because of the threat to the harbour from pirates, and the Fortress San Salvador de la Punta, built in the 16th century. The University of Havana was established in 1728.
hawaii: Hawaii consists of 137 volcanic islands that make up almost the entire Hawaiian archipelago, spanning 1,500 miles in the Pacific Ocean about 2,000 miles southwest of the U.S. mainland. The eight main islands, from northwest to southeast, are Niʻihau, Kauaʻi, Oʻahu, Molokaʻi, Lānaʻi, Kahoʻolawe, Maui and Hawaiʻi, after which the state is named. The archipelago is physiographically and ethnologically part of Polynesia. The name Hawaiʻi is very similar to Proto-Polynesian *Sawaiki, reconstructed as meaning homeland, and one explanation names it for Hawaiʻiloa, a figure of oral tradition said to have discovered the islands.

The date of human arrival is debated. Early archaeological studies suggested Polynesians from the Marquesas or Society Islands arrived as early as the 3rd century CE. Some archaeologists think a later wave from Tahiti around 1100 CE introduced a new line of high chiefs, the kapu system, human sacrifice and the building of heiau, as Hawaiian tradition tells of Paʻao. Others say no evidence supports a later influx and treat Paʻao as myth, and more recent studies place the first settlement at around 900 to 1200 CE. The islands were home to numerous independent chiefdoms.

In 1778 the British explorer James Cook was the first known non-Polynesian to arrive. European and American explorers, traders and whalers followed, and introduced diseases such as syphilis, tuberculosis, smallpox and measles. The indigenous population fell from an estimated 300,000 in the 1770s to 60,000 in the 1850s and 24,000 in 1920, though estimates of the pre-contact figure range from 150,000 to 1.5 million. Hawaii became a unified, internationally recognised kingdom in 1810.

Sugar plantations had a strong foothold by the 1840s and were tightly controlled by American missionary families and businessmen known as the Big Five. In 1893 resident American and European capitalists and landholders overthrew the monarchy. Hawaii was an independent republic from 1894 until 12 August 1898, when it became a U.S. territory. It was attacked by Japan on 7 December 1941 and admitted as a state on 21 August 1959. In 1993 the U.S. government formally apologised for its role in the overthrow.

Hawaii is the 50th state of the United States, with its capital and largest city, Honolulu, on Oʻahu, where two thirds of residents live. Hawaiian was added to the state constitution in 1978 as an official language alongside English. Kamehameha III chose Honolulu as capital for its natural harbour, the present-day Honolulu Harbor, and the previous capitals were Lahaina on Maui and Kailua-Kona on Hawaiʻi. The aboriginal culture is Polynesian, and lūʻau and hula have spread in modified form to the wider United States.
hawiye: The Hawiye trace their lineage to Sheikh Ahmed bin Abdulrahman bin Uthman, known as Sheikh Hawiye. Oral tradition and Arabic hagiologies remember him as a saint called Hawi al-Ulum, conservator of knowledge, a name shortened in time to Hawiye, and carry his genealogy back to Aqeel bin Abu Talib. Some scholars regard such claims as historically untenable. The anthropologist Ioan Lewis held that traditions of descent from noble Arab families are most probably figurative expressions of the importance of Islam in Somali society. Tradition places his tomb at Qundhuro in the Haraghe region, where his eldest son Karanle is buried beside him.

The 12th-century writer Al-Idrisi placed the Hawiye on the coast between Ras Hafun and Merca and in the lower basin of the Shabelle river, the first documentary reference to a specific Somali group. Ibn Sa'id, who lived from 1214 to 1274, called Merca their capital.

In the 13th century the Hawiye, with the Rahanweyn, came under the Ajuran Empire, whose domain reached from Hobyo in the north to Qelafo in the west and Kismayo in the south. The Ajuran are themselves said to descend from the Jambelle branch of the Hawiye, and Lee Cassanelli describes Ajuran power as resting on spiritual pre-eminence and Hawiye kinship solidarity.

According to local oral tradition as Cassanelli reports it, the Hiraab Imamate was an alliance of closely related groups of the Gorgaarte division. Its founders rebelled because the Ajuran rulers had grown proud, neglected sharia law and imposed heavy taxes. With Mogadishu as its capital, the imamate ruled from the Shabelle valley and the Benadir to the arid lands of Mudug for at least two centuries. The explorer John Kirk, visiting in 1873, met Imam Mahmood at Mogadishu and saw about twenty large dhows there and at Merca loading grain, much of it for Zanzibar.

At independence in 1960 the first president, Aden Adde, the first prime minister, Abdullahi Issa, and the founder of the army, Daud Abdulle Hirsi, were all Hawiye. Hawiye leaders formed the United Somali Congress in opposition to President Siad Barre, whom General Mohamed Farrah Aidid, of the Habar Gidir, overthrew in 1991. From late 1991 Mogadishu was divided between the factions of Aidid and of President Ali Mahdi Muhammad, of the Abgaal. The stalemate lasted until 2006, when the Islamic Courts Union, a predominantly Hawiye organisation, ended the rule of the factional warlords, before an Ethiopian intervention overthrew it. The Hiraab hereditary leadership survives to this day.
hebrew: Hebrew is a Northwest Semitic language and belongs to the Canaanite languages. It was the spoken language of the Iron Age kingdoms of Israel and Judah from about 1200 to 586 BCE, and epigraphic evidence supports the view that the earlier layers of biblical literature reflect their language. The earliest examples of written Paleo-Hebrew date to the 10th century BCE. Two claims for older inscriptions are disputed: Amihai Mazar called a shard from Khirbet Qeiyafa, which its discoverer Yossi Garfinkel thought might be the earliest Hebrew writing, proto-Canaanite, and a claimed curse tablet from Mount Ebal is rejected by practically all professional epigraphers apart from its discoverer's team.

Nearly all the Hebrew Bible is written in Biblical Hebrew, much of it in a dialect that scholars believe flourished around the 6th century BCE. For this reason Jews have called it Lashon Hakodesh, 'the holy tongue', since ancient times. The Bible itself calls it Yehudit, 'Judean', and the name Ivrit appears in the Mishnah. Hebrew is written from right to left in an abjad of 22 letters. The ancient Paleo-Hebrew alphabet resembled the Canaanite and Phoenician ones, while the modern 'square' script, Ashurit, developed from the Aramaic script.

Scholars debate how far Hebrew remained a spoken vernacular after the Babylonian exile, when Old Aramaic was the predominant international language. It ceased to be a regular spoken language between 200 and 400 CE, as it declined after the unsuccessful Bar Kokhba revolt against the Roman Empire. It survived as the language of Jewish liturgy, rabbinic literature, commerce between Jews of different native languages and poetry. The first dated book printed in Hebrew was published by Abraham Garton in Reggio in 1475. With the rise of Zionism in the 19th century it was revived as a spoken language, led by Eliezer Ben-Yehuda, and Modern Hebrew became the main language of the Yishuv in Palestine and then the official language of the State of Israel.
hector-berlioz: Hector Berlioz was born on 11 December 1803 at La Côte-Saint-André, in the département of Isère, the eldest child of Louis Berlioz, a physician. He moved to Paris in 1821, aged seventeen, and at his father's insistence enrolled in the School of Medicine, forcing himself to continue despite his revulsion at dissecting bodies. In 1824 he composed a Messe solennelle, which was performed twice and then suppressed; a copy was found in 1991. His first opera, Les Francs-juges, was never performed and survives in fragments, the best known being its overture.

Berlioz won the Prix de Rome in 1830 with the cantata La Mort de Sardanapale, having modified his natural style to please the judges after his Cléopâtre of the previous year had been thought to betray dangerous tendencies. In the same year he wrote the Symphonie fantastique, in which an idealised portrait of the Irish actress Harriet Smithson recurs as an idée fixe. After a concert on 9 December 1832 she finally met him, and they married; the marriage foundered, and she died in June 1862.

In the 1840s he struggled as a composer, completing the song cycle Les Nuits d'été to poems by Théophile Gautier and publishing articles on orchestration that became his Treatise on Instrumentation. After the failure of La Damnation de Faust he turned increasingly to conducting, appearing in London from 1851 and in Germany.

Berlioz called four large works symphonies, but his idea of the genre differed greatly from the classical German pattern, since he used the symphony to tell a story. His three completed operas were never written to commission. Benvenuto Cellini was an outright failure, and Les Troyens, a five-act, five-hour work, was too large for the Opéra: only its last three acts were staged in Paris, in November 1863, and were cut further during a run of 22 performances. The experience demoralised him, and he wrote almost no more music.

Opinion was divided for many years between those who thought him an original genius and those who found his music lacking in form. When Richard Strauss revised the Treatise on Instrumentation in 1905 he added new material but left Berlioz's text unchanged. Berlioz died in Paris on 8 March 1869, aged 65.
heidelberg: Heidelberg lies on the eastern edge of the Upper Rhine Plain, where the Neckar leaves its narrow valley between the Odenwald and the Little Odenwald and begins its last stretch towards Mannheim, about 20 kilometres downstream, where it joins the Rhine. The old town lies in the valley on the south bank, dominated by the ruins of the castle, 80 metres above the river on the slopes of the Königstuhl. On the north bank rises the Heiligenberg, or Holy Mountain, along which runs the Philosophers' Walk.

Between 600,000 and 200,000 years ago, Heidelberg Man died at nearby Mauer; his jaw bone, found in 1907, is the earliest evidence of human life in Europe. In the 5th century BCE a Celtic refuge and place of worship was built on the Heiligenberg, and a fort followed around 40 CE. The first reference to Heidelberg itself is in a document of Schönau Abbey dated 1196, taken as the town's founding date. In 1156 the castle and its settlement passed to the house of Hohenstaufen, and in 1214 the Palatinate passed to Ludwig I, Duke of Bavaria. In 1356 the Golden Bull confirmed far-reaching rights for the counts palatine, who were also electors.

The university played a leading part in scholasticism, Renaissance humanism and the German Reformation, and in April 1518 Martin Luther was received there to defend his Ninety-five Theses. The library, founded in 1421, is the oldest existing public library in Germany. The castle on the higher slope was destroyed by a gunpowder explosion in 1537. Heidelberg fell to the Grand Duchy of Baden in 1803, and Grand Duke Charles Frederick re-founded the university, naming it Ruperto-Carola after its two founders. The university reopened in 1945 on the initiative of a small group of professors, among them Alfred Weber and Karl Jaspers.

Heidelberg is the fifth-largest city in Baden-Württemberg, with about 163,000 inhabitants, roughly a quarter of them students. It belongs to the Rhine-Neckar Metropolitan Region, centred on Mannheim. It is a scientific centre, home to the European Molecular Biology Laboratory and four Max Planck Institutes, and has been named a City of Literature by UNESCO's Creative Cities Network.
heinrich-heine: Heine was born on 13 December 1797 in Düsseldorf, then in the Duchy of Berg, the eldest of four children of the textile merchant Samson Heine and Peira, née van Geldern. He was called Harry in childhood. His uncle Salomon realised that he had no talent for trade, and it was decided that he should study law, so in 1819 he went to the University of Bonn. There he was a radical liberal, but he was more interested in history and literature, heard the critic August Wilhelm Schlegel lecture, and began to acquire a reputation as a poet. He also wrote two tragedies, Almansor and William Ratcliff, which had little success in the theatre.

It was extremely difficult to make a living as a writer in Germany, and Heine never had enough money. In Hamburg in January 1826 he met Julius Campe, who remained his chief publisher for the rest of his life. Books under 320 pages had to be submitted to censorship, so Campe printed dissident works in large type to run longer. Heine's travel writings, the Reisebilder, were a success. He left for France in 1831, drawn by the July Revolution, by freedom from German censorship and for a time by Saint-Simonianism. In Paris he became a celebrity, counting Victor Hugo, Frederic Chopin and Franz Liszt among his acquaintances, and wrote everything in German, translating it into French with a collaborator.

After the German Diet banned the Young Germany writers in November 1835, his name was added at Metternich's insistence, but he went on commenting on German politics from a distance. In the 1840s his verse became more political and satirical. The most popular of his political poems was The Silesian Weavers, based on the weavers' uprising of 1844.

In May 1848 Heine fell paralysed and did not leave what he called his mattress-grave until his death on 17 February 1856. A hair analysis in 1997 confirmed chronic lead poisoning. Many composers set his poems, among them Robert Schumann in the song cycle Dichterliebe and Friedrich Silcher in his setting of Die Lorelei. The Nazis removed or destroyed all monuments to him and, from 1940, banned his books. His line from Almansor, spoken after the burning of the Quran at Granada, was engraved at the site of the 1933 book burning on Berlin's Opernplatz.
helicopter: The fourth-century Daoist book Baopuzi by Ge Hong reportedly describes some of the ideas inherent to rotary-wing aircraft. Designs similar to the Chinese toy appeared in some Renaissance paintings, and in the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries Western scientists developed flying machines based on it. The word helicopter is adapted from the French hélicoptère, coined by Gustave Ponton d'Amécourt in 1861 from the Ancient Greek helix, spiral, and pteron, wing.

Engines held back the early machines. Rubber bands and similar devices limited them to toys and small models, and steam engines lacked the power for manned flight. The internal combustion engine at the end of the nineteenth century made lifting humans possible. In the early 1920s the Argentine Raúl Pateras-Pescara de Castelluccio demonstrated one of the first successful applications of cyclic pitch.

A helicopter's rotor consists of a mast, hub and blades. The torque of a single main rotor must be countered, and the design Igor Sikorsky settled on for his VS-300 was a smaller tail rotor at the end of a tail boom. Between 1939 and 1943 the VS-300 went through four iterations and became the basis for modern helicopters. Twin-rotor designs carry more payload, and coaxial, tiltrotor and compound helicopters also fly. The pilot works the cyclic, the collective, the anti-torque pedals and the throttle, and hovering is the most demanding task. If the engine fails, the helicopter can enter autorotation.

Heinrich Focke designed the transverse twin-rotor Fw 61, which first flew in June 1936. Hanna Reitsch flew it inside the Deutschlandhalle in Berlin in February 1938, and it set records between 1937 and 1939. On 11 December 1951 Charles Kaman's K-225 became the first turbine-powered helicopter. Because it can take off and land vertically and hover, a helicopter does work that was impossible or slow for other aircraft, including transport, military roles, firefighting, search and rescue, medical transport and aerial observation.
helmut-kohl: Helmut Kohl was born on 3 April 1930 in Ludwigshafen, the third child of Hans Kohl, a Bavarian army veteran and civil servant, and Cäcilie Kohl. He joined the Christian Democratic Union in 1946, at the age of 16. In 1958 he took a doctorate in history at Heidelberg University, and then worked for a foundry and for the Industrial Union for Chemistry.

He was elected the youngest member of the Rhineland-Palatinate parliament in 1959. On 19 May 1969 he became minister-president of that state. As a reformer he focused on schools and education: his government abolished school corporal punishment and the parochial school, and he founded the University of Trier-Kaiserslautern. In 1973 he was elected national chairman of the CDU.

Kohl led the opposition under Chancellor Helmut Schmidt. The Free Democratic Party broke with its coalition partner in 1982, and on 1 October 1982 a constructive vote of no confidence deposed Schmidt, the only time a chancellor has been removed in that way. Three days later the Bundestag elected Kohl chancellor of a CDU/CSU-FDP coalition. His government stationed NATO mid-range missiles despite strong opposition from the peace movement.

On 22 September 1984 Kohl met the French president François Mitterrand at Verdun, and their long handshake became a symbol of Franco-German reconciliation. After the revolutions of 1989 his government acted decisively, and reunification followed in 1990. With Mitterrand he was an architect of the Maastricht Treaty, which established the European Union and the euro. He moved the federal capital from Bonn back to Berlin, though government offices relocated only in 1999. He lost the 1998 election to Gerhard Schröder and resigned as party leader.

In 1999 it emerged that the CDU had received and kept illegal donations during Kohl's leadership; Der Spiegel reported that he had not benefited personally but had run the party's finances outside the legal boundaries. His reputation suffered in Germany, though abroad he was still regarded as a European statesman. In 1998 the European heads of state or government named him Honorary Citizen of Europe, an honour previously given only to Jean Monnet. Kohl died on 16 June 2017 in Ludwigshafen, aged 87, and was buried in Speyer after a European act of state in Strasbourg.
henan: Henan means south of the river, the river being the Yellow River, though changes in its course and in administrative boundaries mean that about a quarter of the province now lies north of it. The province is also abbreviated Yu, after Yuzhou, the name of the region in the ancient system of nine provinces. Most of it forms part of the North China Plain, called the breadbasket of China, with floodplains in the east and mountains in the west. The Yellow River enters from the north-west, and its silt has raised the river bed and caused floods that shaped the region. Mount Song and its Shaolin Temple lie near Zhengzhou.

Prehistoric cultures such as the Yangshao and Longshan were active in what is now northern Henan. The later Erlitou culture has been controversially identified with the Xia dynasty. The Shang dynasty, from about 1600 to about 1046 BCE, had its capitals in the province, and the oracle bone inscriptions found at Yinxu in Anyang give insight into its writing, rituals and social structure. After the Zhou overthrew the Shang at the Battle of Muye, the political centre moved away from Henan for the first time. Under the Han, Luoyang became the political and cultural heart of the empire.

Henan passed repeatedly between rival regimes from 220 to 589, yet remained an agricultural base. Emperor Yang of Sui had the Grand Canal extended to Luoyang. In the Five Dynasties period Kaifeng became the capital of four dynasties, and under the Song, who reunified China in 982, Kaifeng overtook Luoyang and Chang'an as the largest city in China and in the world. In 1127 the Jurchens captured Kaifeng and took the Song emperor prisoner, and in 1194 the Yellow River changed course, displacing millions.

After the rebel Li Zicheng took Luoyang in 1641, his forces besieged Kaifeng three times. During the third, Ming troops breached the Yellow River dikes to flood the rebels. The water submerged the city, and of its 378,000 residents only 30,000 survived. A dike breach at Zhengzhou on 30 September 1887 killed over two million people by one account, with estimates from 930,000 to 7 million. In 1938 the government led by Chiang Kai-shek bombed the Huayuankou dam to halt the Japanese advance, causing floods that killed hundreds of thousands. A famine followed in 1942–43.

Henan is a province of central China with Zhengzhou as its capital. Four historical capitals of China, Luoyang, Anyang, Kaifeng and Zhengzhou, lie within it. It has a population of over 99 million, the third largest of any province and the largest among inland provinces. The capital moved from Kaifeng to Zhengzhou in 1954 because of the city's importance for rail transport.
henri-matisse: Henri Émile Benoît Matisse was born on 31 December 1869 in Le Cateau-Cambrésis in northern France, the oldest son of a wealthy grain merchant. In 1887 he went to Paris to study law and afterwards worked as a court administrator. He began to paint in 1889, when his mother brought him art supplies while he was convalescing from appendicitis, and decided to become an artist, which deeply disappointed his father. In 1891 he returned to Paris to study at the Académie Julian under William-Adolphe Bouguereau and at the École Nationale des Beaux-Arts under Gustave Moreau.

The intensity of colour in the works Matisse painted between 1900 and 1905 brought him notoriety as one of the Fauves, French for wild beasts. The movement lasted only from 1904 to 1908, and he and André Derain were its leaders. In 1904 he painted at St. Tropez with the neo-Impressionists Signac and Henri-Edmond Cross, and in 1905 he worked with Derain at Collioure. Around April 1906 he met Pablo Picasso, eleven years younger, and the two became lifelong friends and rivals. Americans in Paris, among them the Stein family and the Cone sisters of Baltimore, collected his work.

In 1917 Matisse moved to Cimiez, a suburb of Nice. His work of the next decade relaxed and softened, though some critics found his odalisque paintings shallow and decorative, and after 1930 a bolder simplification appeared. He was in Paris when the Germans invaded France in June 1940 but returned to Nice and stayed, though his son Pierre begged him to leave.

Diagnosed with abdominal cancer in 1941, Matisse underwent surgery that left him often bedridden. With assistants he began to make cut paper collages from sheets pre-painted with gouache, and the pieces grew into murals and room-sized works. In 1948 he began designs for the Chapelle du Rosaire at Vence, and after 1951 the paper cut-out was his only medium. He called his last years his second life. He died of a heart attack on 3 November 1954, aged 84, and is buried at Cimiez. The Matisse Museum at Le Cateau was established in 1952 and the Musée Matisse in Nice opened in 1963.
henrik-ibsen: Henrik Johan Ibsen was born on 20 March 1828 into an affluent merchant family in the port town of Skien in Telemark. His father, Knud Plesner Ibsen, was a timber and luxury goods merchant, and his mother, Marichen Cornelia Martine Altenburg, belonged like him to the extended Paus family, which had held wealth and power in Telemark since the mid-1500s. Older biographies pictured a descent from privilege into hardship, with a failed and tyrannical father, but a later reading finds this romanticised. At fifteen Ibsen left school and became an apprentice pharmacist in Grimstad, where he began writing plays. His first play, the tragedy Catilina, was published in 1850 under a pseudonym but not performed.

Ibsen established himself as a theatre director in Norway during the 1850s, though the many plays he wrote in those years were unsuccessful. In 1864 he left Christiania for Sorrento and spent the next 27 years in Italy and Germany, mostly in Rome, Dresden and Munich, before returning to Christiania in 1891. Brand and Peer Gynt, the second with incidental music by Edvard Grieg, brought him critical acclaim and some financial success. After Peer Gynt he abandoned verse for realistic prose, and he came to treat what he called the drama of ideas.

His plays from A Doll's House of 1879 onward, among them Ghosts, An Enemy of the People, The Wild Duck, Rosmersholm and Hedda Gabler, examined the morals and family life of the middle class and caused an uproar not only in Norway but across Europe and in America. Many of them are set in Norwegian bourgeois surroundings resembling Skien, and he took names and characters from his own relatives. Critics often rate The Wild Duck and Rosmersholm his best work, while Ibsen himself regarded Emperor and Galilean as his masterpiece.

Ibsen died at his home in Kristiania on 23 May 1906, after a series of strokes that began in March 1900. When his nurse told a visitor on the previous day that he was a little better, his last word was the reply Tvertimod, meaning On the contrary. He was buried in Vår Frelsers gravlund in Oslo. By 2014 he was the most frequently performed dramatist in the world after Shakespeare, and he influenced writers such as George Bernard Shaw, Oscar Wilde and James Joyce. His son Sigurd Ibsen became prime minister of Norway.
henryk-sienkiewicz: Henryk Sienkiewicz was born on 5 May 1846 at Wola Okrzejska in the Kingdom of Poland, then part of the Russian Empire. His family were impoverished Polish nobles, on his father's side descended from Lipka Tatars who had settled in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. He grew up on family estates and in Warsaw, where he studied at the Imperial University and moved from medicine and law to the Institute of Philology and History. He finished in 1871 without a diploma, having failed the examination in Ancient Greek, and lived in poverty as a part-time tutor.

He debuted as a journalist in 1869 and wrote under the pen name Litwos. In 1876 he went to the United States with the actress Helena Modrzejewska, and Gazeta Polska paid for his journey in exchange for travel essays, which won him a popular following. He stayed in California and returned to Poland in 1879. From 1883 he turned to historical novels. With Fire and Sword was serialised from 1883 to 1884, The Deluge from 1884 to 1886 and Sir Michael from 1887 to 1888. Together these make the Trilogy, which established him as the most popular contemporary Polish writer.

He wrote the first chapters of Quo Vadis in February 1895, and the novel was finished by March 1896 and soon gained international renown. He began serialising Krzyżacy, The Teutonic Knights, in 1897, and it was finished in 1900. In 1900 the Polish people gave him an estate at Oblęgorek near Kielce, where he later opened a school for children.

Poland remained partitioned between Russia, Austria and Prussia, later Germany, and Sienkiewicz used his fame to influence world opinion for the Polish cause. He criticised the policy of Germanization of the Polish minority in Germany, supported the Września schoolchildren in 1901, and in 1907 appealed to the intellectual community amid German attempts to expropriate Polish land. A moderate, he declined to stand for the Russian Duma and gave to struggling writers.

In 1905 he won the Nobel Prize in Literature for his merits as an epic writer. In his acceptance speech he said that Poland had been pronounced dead and that the prize was proof that she lived. He died on 15 November 1916.
heraclitus: Little is known of the life of Heraclitus. He was the son of Blyson and came from the Ionian city of Ephesus, a port on the Cayster River on the western coast of Asia Minor, which was then part of the Persian Empire. Ephesus appears to have kept a close relationship with Persia; when Darius the Great suppressed the Ionian revolt in 494 BCE, Ephesus was spared, while Miletus, home of the earlier philosophers, was sacked.

The main source for his life is the doxographer Diogenes Laërtius, whose information is mostly unreliable. His story that Heraclitus gave up the hereditary title of king to his younger brother may at least suggest an aristocratic family. Heraclitus appears to have had little sympathy for democracy or the masses.
